messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 38-year-old history teacher, presented for therapy eight months after being mugged while walking home from a faculty dinner. He described himself as being caught in a loop he couldn't escape, a state of constant, exhausting vigilance that was beginning to erode his marriage and his career. The event itself had been brutally simple. He was on a busy, loud street just a few blocks from his apartment when two men grabbed him from behind. One pinned his arms while the other went through his pockets, the noise of the city traffic and late-night crowds swallowing his shouts for help. He remembered the rough scrape of the pavement against his cheek as they shoved him to the ground, and the coppery taste of blood mixing with grit in his mouth. What haunted him most was the stream of indifferent faces that passed by, a river of people who saw and did nothing.

In the months that followed, the world outside his classroom began to feel like a series of ambushes waiting to happen. The memory of the attack was not a fading image but a recurring, full-body experience. A locker slamming shut in the school hallway, a sudden loud noise, would be enough to trigger it. Instantly, he would be back on the pavement, the phantom taste of blood and dirt flooding his mouth, the memory forcing its way into his mind with an uncontrollable, sensory vividness. Because the memory felt so viscerally real, the world began to feel saturated with potential reminders of it; the press of a crowd on the sidewalk, the sound of men's voices behind him, or even the rough texture of a brick wall against his hand could now feel like a direct threat. These intrusions were terrifyingly real, and each time one occurred, his body would react as if the assault were happening all over again. His heart would pound, and he would immediately begin scanning the faces of his own students, studying their expressions and body language for any sign of a threat. His eyes would dart to the classroom door, the fire escape, calculating his route out before he was even consciously aware of what he was doing.

This constant state of high alert only served to reinforce his deepest convictions. The ceaseless scanning and the startling jolt he felt whenever a student made an unexpected movement nearby solidified his belief that the world is an irredeemably dangerous place. This feeling of imminent threat made him even more sensitive to his triggers; because he was always on guard, the ordinary chaos of a crowded school became a minefield of potential reminders. The daily crush of students in the corridors felt menacing, and carpooling with a colleague, something he used to enjoy, now felt like being trapped in a small, fast-moving box with no control. The experience of being in a crowd or a car with others would immediately bring to mind his appraisal that he was utterly unsafe.

His thoughts increasingly circled around the profound injustice of what had happened. He would lie awake at night, ruminating on how the social contract had failed him, how the police report felt like a perfunctory piece of paperwork, and how the people who should have helped had simply walked on by. This sense of institutional failure and deep unfairness became a trigger in itself, a mental pathway that led directly back to the memory of the attack, making it feel more present and potent. In turn, each time the memory returned with its full sensory horror, it cemented his belief that he had been abandoned and that the world was not a place where one could expect protection or justice. The memory didn't just replay the event; it re-affirmed his darkest conclusions about the world.

The cycle has become relentless. A trigger, like the noise of a crowd, brings back the memory. The memory feels so real it activates his threat system, causing him to scan for exits and danger. This constant hypervigilance reinforces his belief that the world is a dangerous place, and this belief makes him dwell on the injustice of it all, which in turn makes the memory more accessible and intrusive. It was after a school assembly, when a popped balloon sent him into a full-blown panic attack in front of his colleagues, that his wife insisted he seek help. Mark now sits in the therapy room, exhausted and ashamed. He is terrified that he will never feel safe again, that the man he was—the confident teacher, the relaxed husband—is gone for good, replaced by this frightened, watchful stranger.
